input: It is recommended that a three-month pilot should be carried out on 14 pumps at a cost of $45k, with the reliability engineering group taking ownership of the pilot and reporting back before the March capital review. Importantly, the decision on full installation should be held until those pilot results have been reported and considered. The background to this recommendation is that the plant operates 180 pumps, and maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a total of 1297 h of unplanned downtime. Of those downtime hours, bearing failures account for 52%, which suggests that a substantial share of the problem is concentrated in one failure category. Against that background, a sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $432k installed, plus a further $78k per year. By comparison, the proposed pilot involves a much smaller initial commitment of $45k, as opposed to the full installation figure of $432k installed plus $78k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 20%, although it should be noted that this is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. Overall, the pilot is presented as the appropriate next step before any wider commitment covering all 180 pumps is made. The pilot is limited in scope, but the question it answers is the full-installation question, and that is why its results are tied to the March capital review.
target: Run the pilot on 14 pumps for $45k over three months. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. Maintenance records for 12 months are the evidence base for the recommendation. The plant runs 180 pumps, the records show 1297 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 52% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $432k installed, plus $78k per year. The trade-off is therefore a $45k pilot against a full installation quoted at $432k installed plus $78k per year, with the pilot taken first and the full decision held. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 20%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. The pilot is the step that produces plant evidence in place of the vendor figure. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so a downtime change in the pilot cannot be credited to a change in spare-part supply. The March report closes the pilot stage: the reliability engineering group reports the results, and only then is the held decision on full installation taken. The pilot design matches the evidence gap. The records identify where downtime is concentrated, but they do not show what sensors will change at this plant. A bounded pilot creates that missing evidence while the full-installation decision remains open, and the report date ties the evidence to the capital review at which the larger commitment would be considered. The recommendation commits the pilot cost and the reporting date. It does not commit the installed cost for all 180 pumps or the annual charge.
